title: Skewer Party!
reviewNotes: Three branches, 18 exact positions from the six-piece phase after ...Rxf6 at three seconds. Re6+ is a checking rook sacrifice, diverting Rf6 to e6. Qa6+ and forcing queen checks produce the seventh-rank Qb7/Qa7 skewers or the c3–g7 diagonal skewer after ...Ke5. Two selected captures yield exact queen-versus-rook wins; the backtracking branch stops at the checked winning skewer. Earlier seven-piece capture remains source context, not part of the encoded tree.
transcript: Black's brilliant idea is to take this rook because now this is going to attack the white queen. And if white is careless and defends the queen like this, now black is actually winning after a series of precise checks that is going to lead to winning the rook and the game. But white is not that naive and it knows that defending with the rook would fail. And it realizes that queen to C1 would simply lead to a draw. Black king will have to move. And now after a few more checks, we're able to swap the rooks. And now both sides only have one queen left. And this is a drawn end game. But white is not only not naive, white is an actual genius. And it realizes that he is completely winning here thanks to an incredible resource. You see, in chess, material balance is only one part of the story. What truly matters at the end of the day is calculation and concrete lines. And in this position, white can actually win thanks to the incredible and amazing sacrifice. Rook to E6. Sacrificing one of the last two [music] pieces that white has left on the board, creating a massive piece imbalance. Black is up a full rook and surely winning. And by the way, of course, black cannot refuse the sacrifice because then we are going to win the rook. But after this capture, it seems like black is simply out of the woods. What does white possibly have in this position? An irregular check is simply going to allow black to find shelter behind the rook and queen and win the game. But white had foreseen the very precise queen to a6 check, forcing the black king to make a very important decision to either come down here or to one of these two squares. Now, if the king comes up to either one of these squares, this is pretty simple. Notice the fact that the black queen is undefended. And so, queen to B7 is going to skewer the king and queen. And after the king [music] moves, we're going to pick up the queen. And with a little bit of technique and precision, white is going to be able to convert the queen versus rook endame. But after queen to a6 check, the king can of course come down. And now there is no skewer. But white can follow up with queen to c4 check, forcing the black king to make yet another decision to either come to e5 or to d6. If the king backtracks and goes back up, now queen to c5 is going to force him to come all the way up. And now queen to A7 is again the same skewer. And finally after king to E5, thanks to the fact that we have forced the rook to move one square, we have now placed the king and queen on this diagonal. And queen to C3 is another skewer.
